scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Users on pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) and pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2) report they cannot
reach each other in either direction. Both hosts can still ping their
own gateways (10.0.0.1 and 10.0.1.1). The NOC insists the fabric is
healthy: every BGP session is Established, all routes are present on
every router, no interface has flapped, and all FRR daemons are
running. Identify what is silently eating the traffic.

injection.action: add a FORWARD DROP rule for pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 transit

post_inject_check.expect: 0% loss   (gateway still OK -- INPUT chain untouched)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: leaf_router_0_0 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 discards every forwarded
  packet with source in 10.0.0.0/24 and destination in 10.0.1.0/24.
  All pc_0_0 traffic must transit leaf_router_0_0 (its only gateway),
  so pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 packets die there. The reverse direction fails
  too, despite matching no rule on its way in: pc_0_1's echo requests
  ARE delivered to pc_0_0, but pc_0_0's replies (src 10.0.0.2, dst
  10.0.1.2) match the rule and are dropped -- a one-directional filter
  breaks bidirectional traffic. Routing and BGP are completely
  healthy; the drop is at the firewall layer. Local delivery to the
  gateway itself uses the INPUT chain, which is untouched, so both
  hosts still ping their gateways.
Localization: leaf_router_0_0
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule
  (-s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24) on leaf_router_0_0
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP` on
  leaf_router_0_0
scenario.fix_spec:
remove the DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 --
`iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP`

bonus-explains-asymmetric-drop: explains that the single directional rule (10.0.0.0/24 -> 10.0.1.0/24) also kills the reverse ping because replies match it

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected component is the host firewall on leaf_router_0_0 (Linux netfilter/iptables), specifically the FORWARD chain. This router is the default gateway for pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2). An explicit iptables rule on leaf_router_0_0 is dropping any forwarded traffic sourced from 10.0.0.0/24 to 10.0.1.0/24:
-A FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP
The packet counters confirm it is actively filtering the attempted traffic (9 packets, 756 bytes dropped), which aligns with the failed pings between the hosts.

Mechanism: When pc_0_0 sends packets to pc_0_1, they enter leaf_router_0_0 and are evaluated by the FORWARD chain; the rule matches and drops them, so nothing reaches the fabric. In the reverse direction, even if pc_0_1 initiates, the return traffic from 10.0.0.0/24 to 10.0.1.0/24 is dropped on leaf_router_0_0, making connectivity appear broken in both directions. Pings to each host’s own gateway still succeed because those hit the INPUT chain, which is ACCEPT.

Localization: Only leaf_router_0_0 shows this rule; spines, super-spine, and leaf_router_0_1 have default-ACCEPT FORWARD chains.

Root cause: A stray/unauthorized iptables inter-subnet drop rule on leaf_router_0_0.

Corrective fix: Remove or adjust the rule on leaf_router_0_0 (e.g., iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP), or flush/replace the FORWARD policy to match intended fabric ACLs and persist the change via configuration management.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly identifies leaf_router_0_0 as the affected device and repeatedly describes the iptables FORWARD rule on that router.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-component: iptables FORWARD DROP / firewall filter
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly names the host firewall (iptables/netfilter) on leaf_router_0_0 and the FORWARD chain DROP rule (-s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP) as the cause.

per_axis.axis: must-recognize-filter-pattern: recognizes healthy routing + healthy BGP with silent forwarding loss as a packet-filter fault, not a routing fault
per_axis.rationale: The report correctly attributes bidirectional packet loss to an iptables FORWARD DROP on leaf_router_0_0 (not routing/BGP) and explains why gateway pings still work.

per_axis.axis: bonus-explains-asymmetric-drop: explains that the single directional rule (10.0.0.0/24 -> 10.0.1.0/24) also kills the reverse ping because replies match it
per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly states the FORWARD rule drops packets with src 10.0.0.0/24 dst 10.0.1.0/24 and explains that return packets from 10.0.0.0/24 to 10.0.1.0/24 are therefore also dropped, causing the observed asymmetric/bidirectional failure.
Recommends deleting the exact iptables DROP rule (or adjusting/flushing the FORWARD chain and persisting the change), which directly corrects the fault.

The investigation log contains the failing ping, host IPs, rp_filter checks, and the exact iptables FORWARD DROP rule (with packet counters) on leaf_router_0_0; the writeup’s causal chain (rule matches forwarded traffic and drops it, breaking bidirectional ping) follows directly. Evidence rules out other routers and rp_filter, so the conclusion and fix are well supported.
